title: Karan Tacker on Why Outsiders in Bollywood Cannot Afford a Single Failure
excerpt: The Special Ops and Khakee star opens up about the persistent bias against TV actors in the film industry, the pushback he has faced on every project, and why the ecosystem needs to change.
body:
• Karan Tacker says outsiders "get written off much quicker" and cannot afford a single flop, while actors from film families continue getting work despite underperformance
  • The actor reveals he faced "massive pushback" on every OTT project — Special Ops, Khakee: The Bihar Chapter, and Bhay — due to his television background
  • Tacker took a seven-year hiatus from acting after leaving TV, waiting for the right role rather than accepting work that wouldn't advance his career
  • He credits director Neeraj Pandey's faith as a turning point, saying without his support, no platform would have wanted to cast him in a lead role

The Outsider's Calculus

Karan Tacker has spent 16 years in the entertainment industry, and he has learned one thing clearly: the margin for error is zero.

"As an actor from outside the fraternity, I can't afford to have a bad job. I can't afford to have a flop. I can't afford to have a weak moment as an actor because I feel like you get written off much quicker than anybody else in the industry would," Tacker told IANS.

The contrast with industry insiders is, in his telling, straightforward. "If there is an actor who is from a film family or is friends within the fraternity, they could probably not deliver great films or their series are not doing well, but still you'll see them time and again getting more work," he said.

A TV Actor's Uphill Battle

Tacker built his name through television, most prominently with the long-running show Ek Hazaaron Mein Meri Behna Hai. When he decided to make the jump to films and streaming, he walked into a wall.

"At the time that I took a break from television, there were only films, and to crack on was very difficult because nobody was launching any new faces. There was a certain perception about actors who came from television. That was a bit of a barrier to jump," he told ANI.

In an exclusive interview with Variety India, Tacker was more blunt about the scale of the problem. "Everyone has such a bias against actors from television. They are very, very clear that if the actor is from TV, they do not want to cast him in a lead role," he said.

"There was massive pushback on Special Ops. There was massive pushback on Khakee: The Bihar Chapter. There was massive pushback even on Bhay."

— Karan Tacker, in Variety India

The pushback came despite results. Khakee: The Bihar Chapter cracked Netflix's global top ten within three days of release and remained there for two years, contributing to an estimated 4% of Netflix's global subscriptions, according to Tacker.

The Seven-Year Wait

After leaving television, Tacker spent seven years away from acting — a period he says people mistake for being jobless. He hosted reality shows during that stretch but refused acting work that didn't serve his career.

"I was very clear that I would act only on the day that I felt I was adding value to my career," he told Variety India. The turning point came with Special Ops, directed by Neeraj Pandey, in which Tacker played intelligence officer Farooq Ali.

"Had I not had Neeraj Pandey's support, I don't think any platform would have wanted to work with me," he said. Pandey continued the partnership with Khakee and Special Ops Season 2.

The Ecosystem Problem

Tacker's critique extends beyond his own experience to the industry's structure. He argues that the media, casting directors, and platforms all reinforce a closed loop.

"Today, even you must be bored with seeing the same five actors everywhere. You are seeing them in films. You are seeing the same people on OTT. There is no sense of newness. Until the entire ethos of the system changes, you will not have new actors coming in," he told Variety India.

"As an outsider, you can't compete with actors from film families. They can pick up the phone and get advice or guidance easily. For us, the first chunk of our careers is just about finding our bearings," he told ANI.

What's Next

Tacker's most recent work includes Bhay: The Gaurav Tiwari Mystery on Amazon, and his film Tanvi: The Great premiered at the Cannes Film Festival. He says he is now getting enough work to be selective, with projects lined up for 2026, though he notes that not every door is open.

"I don't have a godfather. I'm not someone's son. But I keep working," he said.
